query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their mechanical and thermoelastic behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the fraction of HCP-forming elements in refractory high-entropy alloys reduces the dislocation core energy and shear modulus, leading to extended dislocation cores and altered slip system activation. This structural modification enhances ductility at room temperature but simultaneously compromises high-temperature creep strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase, body-centered cubic structured RHEAs. One alloy (TiZrHfNbTa) contains a significant fraction of HCP-forming elements, while the other (VNbMoTaW) is composed entirely of BCC elements.
generation.intervention: A controlled compositional comparison between two RHEA systems: one enriched with HCP elements and one with a purely BCC elemental makeup.
generation.conditions: Compression testing conducted over a temperature range from ambient (to assess ductility) to high temperatures (to evaluate creep strength and thermoelastic behavior), under identical processing and testing protocols.
generation.structural_mediator: The dislocation core structures, which are predicted to be extended in the alloy containing HCP elements (TiZrHfNbTa) versus compact in the purely BCC alloy (VNbMoTaW).
generation.mechanism: The presence of HCP elements lowers the dislocation core energy and the overall shear modulus of the alloy, leading to extended dislocation cores and a shift in the activated slip systems. This results in enhanced ductility at lower temperatures but also reduces the resistance to creep at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline BCC-rich alloy (VNbMoTaW), the HCP-enriched alloy (TiZrHfNbTa) is expected to exhibit lower yield stress, reduced creep strength, and altered slip plane activation, with observable extended dislocation cores under in situ imaging.
generation.baseline: The behavior of the predominantly BCC-structured alloy (VNbMoTaW), which features compact dislocation cores, higher shear modulus, and better creep resistance at high temperatures.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under compressive loading conditions across a temperature range from room temperature (to test for ductility) to temperatures that approach service conditions for ultra-high-temperature applications.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative differences in yield stress, creep rate, and activation energies between the two systems remain uncertain. Further detailed microstructural and mechanical testing is needed to refine the magnitude of these effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform parallel compression tests on TiZrHfNbTa (HCP-enriched) and VNbMoTaW (BCC-rich) alloys over a broad temperature range. Use in situ electron microscopy to image dislocation core structures and assess the activated slip systems. Additionally, measure yield stress, creep rates, and activation enthalpy in each alloy.
measurements: Slip plane analysis via in situ microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HCP-enriched alloy (TiZrHfNbTa) does not exhibit significantly lower dislocation core energy, altered slip system activation, and reduced high-temperature creep resistance compared to the BCC-rich alloy (VNbMoTaW), then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are of interest for ultrahigh-temperature applications. To overcome their drawbacks — low-temperature brittleness and poor creep strength at high temperatures — improved fundamental understanding is needed. Using experiments, theory, and modeling, we investigated prototypical body-centered cubic (BCC) RHEAs, TiZrHfNbTa and VNbMoTaW. The former is compressible to 77 K, whereas the latter is not below 298 K. Hexagonal close-packed (HCP) elements in TiZrHfNbTa lower its dislocation core energy, increase lattice distortion, and lower its shear modulus relative to VNbMoTaW whose elements are all BCC. Screw dislocations dominate TiZrHfNbTa plasticity, but equal numbers of edges and screws exist in VNbTaMoW. Dislocation cores are compact in VNbTaMoW and extended in TiZrHfNbTa, and different macroscopic slip planes are activated in the two RHEAs, which we attribute to the concentration of HCP elements. One such class comprises the RHEAs which, because of their high melting points, have been proposed as candidates for ultrahigh-temperature applications. However, a single-phase RHEA, TiZrHfNbTa, was recently shown to be significantly weaker in creep than CMSX-4 despite the former’s higher melting point. The weakness was ascribed to two factors: faster diffusion in the BCC matrix of the RHEA relative to the FCC matrix of CMSX-4 and a lack of precipitates. Additional research is therefore needed to enhance the creep strength of TiZrHfNbTa, for example, by the introduction of suitable strengthening precipitates. Meanwhile, RHEAs with higher melting points must also be investigated since diffusion will be slower in such materials. One such RHEA is VNbMoTaW, whose melting point is ~500 °C higher than TiZrHfNbTa,,. However, it has a major disadvantage: lack of ductility at room temperature even in compression.
